## Motivation

Alternative splicing generates distinct protein isoforms from the same
gene. These isoforms can differ in their binding domains and therefore
in which partners they interact with, meaning a switch from one isoform
to another can rewire a cell's protein interaction network even when
total gene expression does not change.

IsoNetAnalyzeR makes this rewiring quantifiable. Given a list of
differentially expressed isoforms (up- and down-regulated relative to a
reference condition), it maps each isoform onto a predicted human
protein interaction network, expands a neighbourhood around it via a
virtual pulldown, and then compares the topology of the up- and
down-condition subnetworks across all genes simultaneously.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Installation

Install CRAN packages:

```{r install-cran}
install.packages(c("igraph", "cli", "ggplot2", "ggraph", "ggrepel", "patchwork"))
```

Install Bioconductor packages:

```{r install-bioc}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
BiocManager::install(c("fgsea", "org.Hs.eg.db", "AnnotationDbi"))
```

**Optional** — parallel execution:

```{r install-parallel}
install.packages(c("future", "future.apply"))
```

**Optional** — Excel input:

```{r install-excel}
install.packages("readxl")
```

Install IsoNetAnalyzeR from GitHub:

```{r install-pkg}
devtools::install_github("IsoformAnalysisGroup/IsoNetAnalyzeR", build_vignettes = TRUE)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The session object

Everything in IsoNetAnalyzeR flows through a single S4 session object of
class `IsoNetAnalyzeR`. It holds the interaction network, all analyses,
quick lookups, and network diagnostics. You create one at the start of
every session:

```{r create-session}
library(IsoNetAnalyzeR)

obj <- IsoNetAnalyzeR("my_experiment")
#> Loaded package-internal network: 45231 vertices, 312847 edges.
```

By default the package's built-in predicted human protein interaction
network is loaded automatically. You can supply your own `igraph` object
instead:

```{r custom-network}
obj <- IsoNetAnalyzeR("custom", network = my_igraph)
```

Printing the object gives a compact session summary:

```{r show-session}
obj
#> ── IsoNetAnalyzeR session ─────────────────────────────────────
#> Name       : my_experiment
#> Created    : 2025-03-01 09:14:22
#> Network    : 45231 vertices / 312847 edges  [source: package_internal]
#> Analyses   : 0 stored  [none]
#> Lookups    : 0 stored  [none]
#> Diagnostics: not run
#> ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

### Metadata

Arbitrary key–value metadata can be attached to the session at any time:

```{r metadata}
obj <- set_metadata(obj, "author",    "Jane Doe")
obj <- set_metadata(obj, "condition", "tumour_vs_normal")
obj <- set_metadata(obj, "notes",     "First pilot run")
print_metadata(obj)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Network diagnostics

Before running any analysis it is useful to understand the structure of
the underlying network (degree distribution, connected components,
sticky (non-specific) nodes) so you know what to expect and whether any
nodes should be treated with caution.

Two methods are available for defining the sticky-node threshold:

-   `sticky_method = "quantile"` (default): nodes above the
    `sticky_cutoff` quantile of the degree distribution are flagged.
    `sticky_cutoff = 0.95` flags the top 5% most connected nodes.
-   `sticky_method = "sd"`: nodes whose degree exceeds the mean plus
    `sticky_cutoff` standard deviations are flagged. `sticky_cutoff = 2`
    (the default for this method) flags nodes more than 2 SDs above the
    mean, which is more aggressive on heavy-tailed distributions.

```{r diagnostics}
# Quantile method — top 5% of nodes by degree
obj <- run_network_diagnostics(obj, sticky_method = "quantile", sticky_cutoff = 0.95)

# SD method — nodes more than 2 SDs above mean degree
obj <- run_network_diagnostics(obj, sticky_method = "sd", sticky_cutoff = 2)

diag <- get_network_diagnostics(obj)
diag
```

The six-panel diagnostic figure covers degree distributions at isoform
and gene level, component size structure, isoforms per gene, clustering
vs degree, and gene connectivity status:

```{r plot-diagnostics}
plot_network_diagnostics(obj)
```

Key slots available on the `NetworkDiagnostics` object:

| Slot | Contents |
|---------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| `@network_stats` | One-row data frame: 19 global statistics |
| `@isoform_degree_table` | Per-isoform: `isoform_id`, `gene_id`, `degree` |
| `@gene_degree_table` | Per-gene: `gene_id`, `degree` |
| `@component_table` | Per-component: `component_id`, `n_nodes`, `n_edges` |
| `@clustering_table` | Per-isoform: `degree`, `clustering_coefficient` |
| `@isoform_per_gene_table` | Per-gene: isoform counts by connectivity status |
| `@sticky_isoform_table` | High-degree isoforms above threshold |
| `@sticky_gene_table` | High-degree genes above threshold |

Sticky nodes are those in the upper tail of the degree distribution.
Their presence in a pulldown result does not necessarily indicate
biological relevance — they may be common binders. Check
`diag@sticky_isoform_table` before interpreting seed neighbourhoods.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Input format

The differential pulldown expects a long-format table with three
required columns:

| Column       | Description                                        |
|--------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| `gene_id`    | Gene identifier (e.g. Ensembl gene ID)             |
| `isoform_id` | Transcript ID matching vertex names in the network |
| `direction`  | `"up"` or `"down"` (case-insensitive, trimmed)     |

Extra columns are retained but ignored. You can supply a CSV path, an
Excel path, or a data frame directly:

```{r input-example}
# From a CSV
obj <- run_differential_pulldown(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "de_isoforms.csv", order = 1)

# From a data frame already in R
de_table <- data.frame(
  gene_id    = c("ENSG00000012048", "ENSG00000012048", "ENSG00000139618"),
  isoform_id = c("ENST00000357654", "ENST00000471181", "ENST00000380152"),
  direction  = c("up",             "down",            "up")
)
obj <- run_differential_pulldown(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", de_table, order = 1)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Differential pulldown

`run_differential_pulldown()` is the main analysis function. For each
gene it:

1.  Splits isoforms into up-regulated and down-regulated sets.
2.  Runs a virtual pulldown separately for each set: restricts the full
    network to predicted interaction edges (`interact == 1`), expands
    via BFS up to `order` hops, then filters out nodes whose edges are
    predominantly external to the subnetwork (the `cutoff` parameter).
3.  Computes per-node statistics (degree, clustering, distance from
    seed, interaction confidence) for each direction subgraph.
4.  Assembles a cross-gene summary with 35 columns comparing the two
    subgraphs.

```{r run-pulldown}
obj <- run_differential_pulldown(
  obj,
  label   = "tumour_vs_normal",
  input   = "de_isoforms.csv",
  order   = 1,
  confirm = FALSE   # suppress interactive coverage prompt in scripts
)
```

Before the analysis runs, a **network coverage report** is printed
showing how many of your input isoforms and genes were found in the
network. Isoforms not present in the network are silently skipped — they
do not produce a subgraph, and their gene will be absent from the
cross-gene summary if no other isoform of that gene is found. Genes
where at least one isoform is found but all its interactions have been
filtered will produce a single-node subgraph, which is a valid result.
In interactive sessions `confirm = TRUE` (the default) pauses and asks
you to confirm before proceeding; set `confirm = FALSE` in scripts.

### Parallel execution

For analyses with many genes, parallelism is opt-in via the `future`
package:

```{r parallel}
library(future)
plan(multisession, workers = 4)

obj <- run_differential_pulldown(
  obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "de_isoforms.csv",
  order    = 1,
  parallel = TRUE
)

plan(sequential)
```

### Virtual pulldown parameters

| Parameter | Default | Effect |
|----------------------------|-----------------------|---------------------|
| `order` | 1 | BFS hops from the seed isoforms. `order = 1` includes direct interactors only. |
| `cutoff` | `obj@metadata$network_cutoff` | Minimum fraction of a candidate node's edges that must be internal to the subnetwork. Nodes below this threshold are discarded as non-specific. |

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Accessing results

### Cross-gene summary

The 35-column cross-gene summary has one row per gene and is the primary
starting point for most downstream questions:

```{r cgs}
cgs <- get_cross_gene_summary(obj, "tumour_vs_normal")
```

Selected column groups:

**Topology (per condition):** `up_nodes`, `up_edges`, `up_density`,
`up_avg_degree`, `up_clustering`, `up_starness` (degree centralization;
0 = uniform, 1 = pure hub-and-spoke), `up_genes` and the equivalent
`down_*` columns.

**Node-set overlap:** `n_shared_nodes`, `n_up_unique`, `n_down_unique`,
`jaccard` (Jaccard index of node-set overlap between conditions).

**Edge rewiring:** `n_edges_gained` (in up but not down), `n_edges_lost`
(in down but not up), `n_edges_shared`.

**Interaction confidence (seeds only):** `up_seed_mean_pi` (mean edge
confidence across up seeds), `up_seed_pi_entropy` (Shannon entropy of
confidence distribution — high entropy means many edges of similar
moderate confidence; low entropy means a few high-confidence
interactions).

```{r cgs-explore}
# Most rewired genes
cgs$delta_edges <- cgs$up_edges - cgs$down_edges
head(cgs[order(-abs(cgs$delta_edges)), c("gene_id", "up_edges", "down_edges",
                                          "n_edges_gained", "n_edges_lost", "jaccard")])

# Genes with very different network partners (low Jaccard)
low_overlap <- cgs[!is.na(cgs$jaccard) & cgs$jaccard < 0.1, ]

# Genes where the up condition recruits many more cross-gene partners
cgs[!is.na(cgs$up_genes) & cgs$up_genes > cgs$down_genes + 5, "gene_id"]
```

### Cross-gene plots

Two families of plots read directly from the cross-gene summary table.
The overview functions produce multi-panel patchwork figures; the single
functions let you customise any column pair:

```{r cgs-plots-scatter}
# Six-panel scatter overview (up vs down for nodes, edges, degree, density,
# clustering, and edges gained vs lost)
plot_cross_gene_overview(obj, "tumour_vs_normal")

# Single scatter — any two numeric columns
plot_cross_gene_scatter(obj, "tumour_vs_normal",
                        x_col   = "up_nodes",
                        y_col   = "down_nodes",
                        label_n = 8,
                        label   = "delta")
```

```{r cgs-plots-boxplot}
# Multi-panel boxplot overview of topology deltas
plot_cross_gene_boxplot_overview(obj, "tumour_vs_normal")

# Single boxplot — any two numeric columns as the delta metric
plot_cross_gene_boxplot(obj, "tumour_vs_normal",
                        x_col = "up_edges",
                        y_col = "down_edges")
```

### Per-gene results

For any individual gene you can retrieve per-isoform statistics for both
conditions as a single long-format data frame:

```{r isoform-stats}
iso <- get_isoform_stats(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "ENSG00000012048")
# Returns columns: direction, isoform, is_seed, degree, clustering,
#                  distance_from_seed, mean_pi, pi_entropy

# Seed isoforms only
iso[iso$is_seed, ]

# Up-condition isoforms sorted by degree
up <- iso[iso$direction == "up", ]
up[order(-up$degree), ]
```

The full `GeneDiffPulldown` object (containing the igraph subgraphs) is
retrieved with `get_gene_result()`:

```{r gene-result}
gr <- get_gene_result(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "ENSG00000012048")
gr   # show() summary
```

`plot_network()` dispatches on the object type and exposes several
display modes via the `direction` argument:

-   `"side_by_side"` (default): two-panel patchwork figure showing the
    up and down subgraphs next to each other. Note this produces **two
    panels**, so your plot viewer will show two images.
-   `"overlay"`: merges both subgraphs into one plot. Nodes and edges
    are coloured by membership — up-only (orange), down-only (sky blue),
    or shared (grey). Seed isoforms are shown with a distinct shape.
-   `"up"` / `"down"`: renders a single condition subgraph with seeds
    highlighted.

The `group_by_gene` argument (isoform level only) colours nodes by their
parent gene, useful when several genes share interaction partners:

```{r gene-result-plots}
# Side-by-side (default) — produces two panels
plot_network(gr)

# Side-by-side with nodes coloured by parent gene
plot_network(gr, group_by_gene = TRUE)

# Overlay: up/down/shared membership in one plot
plot_network(gr, direction = "overlay")

# Overlay with gene colouring: fill = gene, border = membership
plot_network(gr, direction = "overlay", group_by_gene = TRUE)

# Single condition
plot_network(gr, direction = "up")

# Gene-level view (isoforms contracted to their parent gene)
plot_network(gr, level = "gene")
```

When called on the full `DifferentialPulldownAnalysis` object,
`plot_network()` builds a merged cross-gene network. The `colour_by`
argument controls how shared nodes are highlighted:

-   `"gene"` (default): nodes coloured by source gene; multi-gene shared
    nodes shown in dark grey with size scaled by degree.
-   `"hub_degree"`: non-shared nodes collapsed to grey; shared nodes
    coloured on a sequential scale by degree, making high-connectivity
    hubs the visual focus.

```{r cross-gene-plot}
result <- get_analysis(obj, "tumour_vs_normal")

# Default: all genes, both directions, coloured by source gene
plot_network(result)

# Focus on shared interaction hubs
plot_network(result, colour_by = "hub_degree", min_shared_nodes = 2)

# Up-regulated subgraphs only, subset to two genes of interest
plot_network(result, direction = "up", genes = c("ENSG00000012048", "ENSG00000139618"))

# Gene-level view, keep only larger components
plot_network(result, level = "gene", min_component_nodes = 5)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Ad hoc virtual pulldown

For single-gene or single-isoform exploration without preparing a full
differential input table, use `lookup_virtual_pulldown()`. One or more
seeds can be supplied; all are treated as order-0 anchors in a single
pulldown.

```{r lookup}
# Single isoform seed
obj <- lookup_virtual_pulldown(
  obj,
  label = "BRCA1_isoform_1",
  seed  = "ENST00000357654",
  order = 1,
  level = "isoform"
)

# Multiple seeds — all anchored at order 0 in one pulldown
obj <- lookup_virtual_pulldown(
  obj,
  label = "BRCA1_combined",
  seed  = c("ENST00000357654", "ENST00000471181"),
  order = 1
)

# Node statistics
stats <- get_lookup_stats(obj, "BRCA1_isoform_1")
stats[stats$is_seed, ]

# The subgraph itself
g <- get_lookup_subgraph(obj, "BRCA1_isoform_1")
igraph::vcount(g)
igraph::ecount(g)

plot_network(get_lookup(obj, "BRCA1_isoform_1"))
```

Gene-level lookup: supply a gene ID and set `level = "gene"` to seed
from all isoforms of that gene simultaneously:

```{r lookup-gene}
obj <- lookup_virtual_pulldown(
  obj,
  label = "BRCA1_gene",
  seed  = "ENSG00000012048",
  order = 1,
  level = "gene"
)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Component analysis

The component analysis merges all per-gene subgraphs into a single
cross-gene network and decomposes it into connected components.
Components containing seeds from both the up and down condition are
flagged as **mixed** — these represent potential rewiring events where
the same interaction neighbourhood is recruited in both conditions but
by different isoforms.

`run_component_analysis()` accepts three filter arguments that are
applied after the merged graph is built. They compose — all three can be
used together:

| Argument | Effect |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `min_component_nodes` | Drop components with fewer total nodes. Use to remove singletons and pairs. |
| `min_shared_nodes` | Drop components with fewer multi-gene shared nodes. The strongest lever for keeping only biologically interesting cross-gene hubs. |
| `min_edges` | Drop components with fewer edges. Removes loosely connected components that pass a node-count threshold but have sparse connectivity. |

The `genes` argument restricts the analysis to a subset of genes, and
`direction` controls whether up-only, down-only, or the union of both
subgraphs is merged. `level = "gene"` contracts isoform nodes to their
parent gene before decomposition:

```{r component-run}
# Default: isoform level, both directions, all genes, no filters
obj <- run_component_analysis(
  obj,
  analysis = "tumour_vs_normal",
  label    = "comp_both"
)

# Keep only components with >= 3 nodes and at least 1 shared hub
obj <- run_component_analysis(
  obj,
  analysis            = "tumour_vs_normal",
  label               = "comp_filtered",
  min_component_nodes = 3,
  min_shared_nodes    = 1,
  min_edges           = 2
)

# Up-regulated subgraphs only, gene-level contraction
obj <- run_component_analysis(
  obj,
  analysis  = "tumour_vs_normal",
  label     = "comp_up_gene",
  direction = "up",
  level     = "gene"
)
```

### Component overview

`get_component_overview()` returns Tier-1 (structural) and Tier-2
(topological) statistics joined into one wide table — one row per
component:

```{r comp-overview}
overview <- get_component_overview(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both")
```

**Tier-1 structural columns:** `n_nodes`, `n_edges`, `density`,
`avg_degree`, `clustering`, `n_seeds`, `n_neighbours`, `seed_fraction`,
`n_seeds_up`, `n_seeds_down`, `n_genes_up`, `n_genes_down`, `mixed`,
`n_shared_nodes`, `shared_fraction`.

**Tier-2 topological columns:** `diameter` (longest shortest path),
`radius` (minimum eccentricity), `degree_centralization` (0 = uniform
degree distribution, 1 = pure star), `topology_class` (`"hub-spoke"`,
`"chain-like"`, or `"clique-like"`).

```{r comp-filter}
# Rewiring candidates: components with both up and down seeds
overview[overview$mixed, c("component_id", "n_nodes", "n_seeds_up",
                            "n_seeds_down", "topology_class")]

# Potential master regulators: hub-spoke topology with shared nodes
hub_spoke <- overview[!is.na(overview$topology_class) &
                        overview$topology_class == "hub-spoke" &
                        overview$n_shared_nodes > 0, ]
hub_spoke[order(-hub_spoke$degree_centralization), ]
```

### Per-component node table

For any component, `get_component()` returns a per-node table with hub
betweenness scores for shared nodes:

```{r comp-node}
nodes <- get_component(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both", component_id = 1)
# columns: component_id, node, source_gene, seed_direction, is_seed, degree,
#          betweenness, betweenness_norm, betweenness_rank

# Nodes bridging across gene communities (high normalised betweenness)
nodes[!is.na(nodes$betweenness_norm) & nodes$betweenness_norm > 0.5, ]
```

`plot_component()` supports three `colour_by` modes:

-   `"direction"` (shown below): seeds coloured orange (up) or blue
    (down). With `colour_neighbours = TRUE`, neighbour nodes are
    coloured by the direction of their nearest seed — revealing which
    territory each isoform condition dominates.
-   `"gene"`: nodes coloured by source gene; shared multi-gene nodes in
    dark grey.
-   `"hub_degree"`: shared nodes coloured by degree on a sequential
    scale, making cross-gene hubs the visual focus.

```{r comp-plot}
# Territory map: up/down seed zones + neighbour colouring
plot_component(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both", component_id = 1,
               colour_by = "direction", colour_neighbours = TRUE)

# Source gene colouring
plot_component(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both", component_id = 1,
               colour_by = "gene")

# Hub focus: shared nodes coloured by degree
plot_component(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both", component_id = 1,
               colour_by = "hub_degree")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Gene set enrichment

### ORA per component

Over-representation analysis tests whether GO terms are enriched in the
gene set of each component, using the full network gene universe as
background. The `go_category` argument selects the GO sub-ontology:

| Value | Ontology |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `"GO:BP"` (default) | Biological process — *what* the proteins do |
| `"GO:MF"` | Molecular function — *how* they act at the molecular level |
| `"GO:CC"` | Cellular component — *where* they are located |
| `"ALL"` | All three ontologies combined |

The `nodes` argument controls whether all component members or seeds
only form the foreground gene set:

```{r ora}
obj <- run_component_ora(
  obj,
  analysis           = "tumour_vs_normal",
  component_analysis = "comp_both",
  label              = "ora_bp",
  go_category        = "GO:BP",
  nodes              = "all"     # or "seeds" to restrict to seed genes only
)

# Also test molecular function
obj <- run_component_ora(
  obj,
  analysis           = "tumour_vs_normal",
  component_analysis = "comp_both",
  label              = "ora_mf",
  go_category        = "GO:MF"
)

# All significant terms across all components
get_ora_table(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both", "ora_bp", padj_cutoff = 0.05)

# Top 3 terms per component — quick biological overview
get_ora_table(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both", "ora_bp", top_n = 3)

# Detailed results for one component
get_ora_table(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both", "ora_bp",
              component_id = 1, padj_cutoff = 0.05)

# Top 5 significant terms for one component — filters compose in order:
# component_id → padj_cutoff → top_n
get_ora_table(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both", "ora_bp",
              component_id = 1, padj_cutoff = 0.05, top_n = 5)
```

For direct access to the full S4 result object (e.g. to inspect run
parameters, the background universe, or slot directly into custom code),
use `get_component_ora_result()`:

```{r ora-result-object}
ora_obj <- get_component_ora_result(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "comp_both", "ora_bp")
ora_obj                 # show() summary: components tested, significant terms
ora_obj@params          # minSize, maxSize, universe_size, n_components_tested
ora_obj@universe        # background gene set used
```

### GSEA on topology deltas

`run_fgsea()` ranks all genes by a topology delta score (e.g. the
difference in node count between up and down subgraphs) and runs fgsea
against GO gene sets. This identifies pathways whose member genes are
systematically gaining or losing network connectivity in one condition.
The `go_category` argument accepts the same options as
`run_component_ora()` (`"GO:BP"`, `"GO:MF"`, `"GO:CC"`, `"ALL"`),
defaulting to `"GO:BP"`.

```{r gsea}
obj <- run_fgsea(
  obj,
  analysis  = "tumour_vs_normal",
  label     = "gsea_nodes",
  rank_by   = "delta_nodes"   # up_nodes - down_nodes
)

# Significant pathways
sig <- get_gsea_table(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "gsea_nodes", padj_cutoff = 0.05)
sig[order(sig$NES), c("pathway", "NES", "padj", "size")]

# The gene ranking used as GSEA input
ranks <- get_gsea_stats(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "gsea_nodes")
head(ranks, 10)   # genes with the largest up-condition network expansion
```

Available `rank_by` presets — all computed as the up-condition metric
minus the down-condition metric, so positive values indicate greater
network expansion in the up condition and negative values indicate the
reverse:

| Preset | Delta computed | Biological interpretation |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `"delta_nodes"` *(default)* | `up_nodes − down_nodes` | Up isoforms recruit more interaction partners |
| `"delta_edges"` | `up_edges − down_edges` | Up subgraph is more densely connected |
| `"delta_avg_degree"` | `up_avg_degree − down_avg_degree` | Up seeds have higher mean connectivity |
| `"delta_density"` | `up_density − down_density` | Up subgraph is more tightly interlinked |
| `"delta_clustering"` | `up_clustering − down_clustering` | Up isoforms form more tightly clustered modules |
| `"delta_starness"` | `up_starness − down_starness` | Up subgraph is more hub-and-spoke shaped |
| `"delta_genes"` | `up_genes − down_genes` | Up isoforms span more distinct gene communities |
| `"delta_seed_mean_pi"` | `up_seed_mean_pi − down_seed_mean_pi` | Up seeds have higher-confidence interactions |
| `"delta_seed_pi_entropy"` | `up_seed_pi_entropy − down_seed_pi_entropy` | Up seeds have more evenly distributed interaction confidence |
| `"edges_gained_vs_lost"` | `n_edges_gained − n_edges_lost` | Net edge rewiring balance |

### Custom gene ranking

If none of the presets fit your question, pass a named numeric vector
directly via the `stats` argument. This completely bypasses `rank_by` —
names must be gene IDs and the vector is used as-is as the fgsea rank
statistic. Genes with `NA` values are silently dropped before running.

```{r gsea-custom}
cgs <- get_cross_gene_summary(obj, "tumour_vs_normal")

# Example: weighted combination of node and edge delta
my_stats <- setNames(
  (cgs$up_nodes - cgs$down_nodes) * 0.7 +
  (cgs$up_edges - cgs$down_edges) * 0.3,
  cgs$gene_id
)

obj <- run_fgsea(
  obj,
  analysis = "tumour_vs_normal",
  label    = "gsea_weighted",
  stats    = my_stats          # rank_by is ignored when stats is supplied
)

get_gsea_table(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "gsea_weighted", padj_cutoff = 0.05)
```

For direct access to the full S4 result object (e.g. to inspect
`@ranked_genes` directly, check `@params`, or extract `@go_category`),
use `get_gsea_result()`:

```{r gsea-result-object}
gsea_obj <- get_gsea_result(obj, "tumour_vs_normal", "gsea_nodes")
gsea_obj                  # show() summary: pathways tested, significant hits
gsea_obj@params           # minSize, maxSize, nperm, n_genes_ranked
gsea_obj@rank_by          # which preset was used (e.g. "delta_nodes")
gsea_obj@ranked_genes     # named numeric vector: gene_id -> delta statistic
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Session management

All analyses and lookups are stored inside the session object under
user-supplied labels. Use the list functions to inspect what has been
run:

```{r list}
list_analyses(obj)   # character vector of analysis labels
list_lookups(obj)    # character vector of lookup labels

# Retrieve a stored analysis object directly
analysis_obj <- get_analysis(obj, "tumour_vs_normal")
```

Sessions can be saved and reloaded with standard R serialisation:

```{r save}
saveRDS(obj, "isonetanalyzer_session.rds")
obj <- readRDS("isonetanalyzer_session.rds")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Typical analysis checklist

1.  `IsoNetAnalyzeR()` — create session
2.  `run_network_diagnostics()` — understand the network; note sticky
    nodes
3.  `run_differential_pulldown()` — core analysis (sequential or
    parallel)
4.  `get_cross_gene_summary()` — identify high-rewiring genes
5.  `plot_cross_gene_overview()` / `plot_cross_gene_boxplot_overview()`
    — visual overview of all topology metrics
6.  `get_isoform_stats()` + `plot_network()` — drill into genes of
    interest
7.  `run_component_analysis()` — decompose the cross-gene network
8.  `get_component_overview()` — filter for mixed / hub-spoke components
9.  `plot_component()` — visualise rewiring within each component
10. `run_component_ora()` + `get_ora_table()` — biological
    interpretation per component
11. `run_fgsea()` + `get_gsea_table()` — pathway-level topology shifts
12. `saveRDS()` — save the session

------------------------------------------------------------------------
